rows.label: Consumption of KIND's clients' families in their home countries, as a share of the national survey mean
rows.explainer: Unaccompanied children come disproportionately from poor, rural and indigenous families (western Guatemala's highlands, Honduras's gang-controlled neighbourhoods), but rarely from the very poorest, since the journey costs thousands of dollars. Anchors: the bottom 40%'s survey mean is 0.32 of the mean in Honduras (3.65 against 11.55 a day) and 0.41 in El Salvador (6.31 against 15.46, World Bank WDI SI.SPR.PC40, 2023); the national mean is the top. Our judgment 0.6, from 0.35 (the bottom 40%) to 1 (the mean). Read by both KIND models.

rows.label: How long a child's higher consumption in the US lasts (years)
rows.explainer: KIND's clients are mostly teenagers (13 to 17); one who stays in the US with status rarely returns, so the gain lasts most of a working life and beyond, about 60 years for a 16-year-old. We count 40 years, from 25 (later returns, and the first years as a dependent spent partly in the sponsor's household) to 55; discounted at the shared rate where read, which makes the later years count little. IRAP's figure for mostly adult refugees is 30 (facts/irap.json); children's is longer. Read by both KIND models.

rows.label: Chance that a child left without legal status is in fact removed from the US
rows.explainer: Most removal orders against children are not carried out: in fiscal year 2014 immigration courts ordered 13,204 minors removed but just 1,863 were deported that year (Migration Policy Institute, 2015), about 14% of a year's orders; an order stays enforceable for life, so the lifetime chance is higher, and enforcement against unaccompanied children rose sharply from 2025 (ICE 'welfare checks' on sponsors). For adults who lose their cases charityevals' model of the IRC's resettlement work takes 50% (30-80%), including those who leave on their own; children are removed less often than adults (ICE rarely removes unaccompanied minors directly from custody). Our judgment 30% over a lifetime, from 10% to 60%. The others stay in the US without status, which the legal-status gain values. Read by both KIND models.

source.title: Migration Policy Institute, Beyond the Surge: Most Unaccompanied Minors Still Await Immigration Court Hearings (press release on its issue brief)
source.quote: In FY 2014, 13,204 minors were ordered removed, but just 1,863 were actually deported.

rows.label: Death rate of young people returned to northern Central America, in the first years back (deaths per person-year)
rows.explainer: Many of KIND's clients fled gang violence and threats, which wait for them on return. Anchors: homicide rates of about 31 per 100,000 in Honduras and 17 in Guatemala in 2023 (El Salvador's fell to about 2 after its 2022 crackdown), with young men at two to four times the national rate; all-cause deaths at ages 15-24 in the region of roughly 1.5 to 2 per 1,000 a year; and documented killings of deportees (Human Rights Watch, Deported to Danger, 2020: 138 Salvadorans killed after deportation from the US, 2013-2019). Our judgment 0.0025, from 0.0012 to 0.005. Read by both KIND models.

rows.label: Death rate of young people of KIND's clients' ages in the US (deaths per person-year)
rows.explainer: US deaths at ages 15 to 24 run at about 0.8 per 1,000 a year (CDC, recent years), higher for young men, lower for younger teens and for Hispanic immigrants; 0.0009, from 0.0006 to 0.0012. Only the excess over it counts. Read by both KIND models.

rows.label: Years a returned young person faces the excess danger
rows.explainer: The targeted threat (the gang a child fled, reprisals against deportees) is highest in the first years after return, and many re-migrate or move within the country; the long-run gap in mortality between Central America and the US beyond that is small at these ages and left out. 3 years, from 1 to 5, discounted where read. IRAP's figure for refugees waiting in danger is the same (facts/irap.json). Read by both KIND models.

rows.label: Share of the deaths averted among KIND's clients that fall at ages 5 to 14
rows.explainer: Most unaccompanied children are 14 to 17 when they arrive and older by the time a case ends, and violence falls mostly on teenagers and young adults; younger children come too (KIND represents children from toddlers up). Our judgment 20%, from 10% to 35%, the rest valued at ages 15-49. Read by both KIND models.
